transcript:
Operator
Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Viper Energy Q3 2025 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message that you're advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again.
Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Chip Seale, Investor Relations Director. Please go ahead.
Chip Seale
Investor Relations Director, Diamondback Energy
Thank you, Amber. Good morning, welcome to Viper Energy's Q3 2025 Conference Call. During our call today, we will reference an updated investor presentation, which can be found on Viper's website. Representing Viper today are Kaes Van't Hof, CEO, and Austen Gilfillan, President. During this conference call, the participants may make certain forward-looking statements relating to the company's financial condition, results of operations, plans, objectives, future performance, and businesses.
We caution you that actual results could differ materially from those that are indicated in these forward-looking statements due to a variety of factors. Information concerning these factors can be found in the company's filings with the SEC. In addition, we will make reference to certain non-GAAP measures. The reconciliations with the appropriate GAAP measures can be found in our earnings release issued yesterday afternoon. I will now turn the call over to Kaes.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Thank you, Chip. Welcome everyone, and thank you for listening to Viper Energy's Q3 2025 conference call. During the Q3, Viper continued to execute on our growth strategy, bolstered by the closing of the Sitio acquisition and continued organic growth. Our Q4 2025 oil production guidance implies a roughly 20% increase in oil production per share compared to the same quarter last year.
Looking ahead to next year, 2026, we continue to anticipate mid-single digit organic oil production growth from Q4 2025 estimated production. This implies double-digit year-over-year growth in oil production per share relative to 2025. Viper also showcased our differentiated return of capital profile in the Q3.
Because of our high operating and free cash flow margins, strong balance sheet and recent signing of our non-Permian asset sale, we felt it appropriate to lean into our return of capital commitment and return 85% of cash available for distribution in Q3 to stockholders. As a result, Viper is delivering on multiple strategic capital allocation fronts this quarter. Our combined base plus variable dividend represents a greater than 6% annualized yield and an increase of almost 10% relative to our dividend from last quarter.
This dividend increase is combined with over $90 million of share repurchases completed during the quarter and an incremental $60 million being retained via the balance sheet. In total, Q3 return of capital per Class A share represents a 48% increase versus Q2.
Looking ahead, as we move to close our non-Permian asset sale and as a result, move closer to our long-term net debt target of $1.5 billion, we will have line of sight to return nearly 100% of cash available for distribution to stockholders. We continue to expect to continue to allocate the majority of our cash for distribution to our base plus variable dividend, feel compelled to buy back shares in today's market given the current market dislocation and unique opportunity to invest countercyclically by increasing our ownership in our existing high-quality mineral and royalty assets.
Importantly, the share repurchases done today will further enhance our growth in per share metrics and allow us to distribute more through our base plus variable dividend over the long term.
On the operational front, we continue to see strong activity levels across our asset base and as a result, continue to expect mid-single digit organic growth in 2026, despite the commodity price volatility we have seen over the past several quarters. Following the closing of the Sitio acquisition, Viper is positioned to benefit from a best of both worlds situation. Viper continues to own concentrated interests under Diamondback's core Midland Basin development, which is expected to drive meaningful long-term oil production growth.
In addition, Viper now has broad exposure to leading third-party operators across both the Midland and Delaware Basins. Our current acreage position has consistently captured almost half of all third-party activity in the Permian. Beyond this, the 25,000 existing horizontal wells in the Permian Basin, in which Viper owns an interest, provides an invaluable information advantage.
In conclusion, we continue to believe that Viper presents a differentiated investment opportunity within the broader energy space. Viper's unmatched ability to deliver sustained per share growth with zero capital and limited operating costs should result in a differential ability to return increasing amounts of capital to stockholders over the long term. Additionally, given our extremely low break-even, our business model should provide a more consistent cash flow returns profile during times of overall market volatility. Operator, please open the line for questions.
Operator
Thank you. At this time, we will conduct the question-and-answer session. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from Neal Dingmann of William Blair. Your line is now open.
Neal Dingmann
Analyst, William Blair
Hey, morning to you, Kaes, and great free cash flow story, obviously. My first question, it just turned into given, you know, the nearly $700 million asset sale and, you know, what should be probably even over $1.5 billion of free cash flow next year. Could you speak to sort of near term in 2026 at capital allocation? I mean, as I see it seems like, you know, you'll not only quickly repay that debt, but, you know, you could bump distributions up materially and potentially do some buybacks. Would love to hear how you're thinking of it.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, Neal, you know, I feel like, you know, we got a great number on that asset sale and we debated internally if we, you know, should wait or execute on the sale. We decided to execute. The reason being, you know, you recall last quarter, we came out and said, when Viper gets to $1.5 billion of net debt, we're gonna return 100% of free cash back to shareholders.
You know, with this asset sale proceeds coming in, you know, we feel like we have line of sight to that goal. Therefore, we're gonna lean in ahead of that by, you know, adding some repurchases to our story, just given how much the market dislocation has widened between Viper and where it should trade.
High level, you know, I think by the beginning of the year next year, we'll be ready to consistently return almost 100% of free cash to shareholders. We're not gonna stop now. We're gonna be a little aggressive as we head into year-end with the buybacks plus a significant continued cash distribution story.
Neal Dingmann
Analyst, William Blair
That kind of leads to my second question. Is that predicated, I guess, or maybe ask another way? Could you just speak to how activity, you know, outside of Diamondback is trending? It seems like judging by last quarter, things still appear very active, even more active than, you know, what we're seeing from some of these operators out there. Really just want to confirm that's still the case.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, I think it's, I think it's really strong. I'll let Austen, you know, give some more detail, but this is the Q1 we're looking at a combined, you know, Viper Energy and Sitio together, and we think that gives us a broad exposure to a lot of the Permian.
Austen Gilfillan
President, Viper Energy
Yeah, I mean, we put some new details in the deck, page 11 being one of those. What this really does is go back to the beginning of 2023 and looks at all of the wells drilled across the Permian Basin, excluding Diamondback, and what percentage of those, you know, Viper's current asset base would own an interest in. What you'll see is that, you know, we've just captured almost half of all activity across the basin over this time period with a pretty consistent average NRI, right around 1.5%.
You know, it'll trend up and down kind of with activity a bit. You know, I really think it speaks to the quality of the acreage and the operators that we have outside of Diamondback deploying consistent capital to this position.
You know, that gives a lot of confidence to the forecast of 2026 and really even beyond that.
Neal Dingmann
Analyst, William Blair
Makes sense. Thanks, boys.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Thanks, Neal.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Betty Jiang of Barclays. Your line is now open.
Betty Jiang
Senior Equity Research Analyst of US Integrated Oil and E&Ps, Barclays
Hi, thanks for taking my question. I wanted to ask about the third-party activity. Also, just on the, I mean, the backlog has continued to increase, but even, I want to understand how much of that increase is driven by the Sitio contribution and how much is seeing a broader constructive uplift that you're seeing across from the legacy assets from other operators across the Permian.
Austen Gilfillan
President, Viper Energy
Yeah, Betty, I would say it's pretty evenly mixed. You know, I think being a couple of months in post-Sitio closing, that asset base has outperformed the underwriting assumptions. Really, Legacy Viper's third-party operated position has continued to outperform as well, mainly as a result of some of the higher NRIs. You can kind of see that showing up on slide 11, as I mentioned.
You know, as we look at it today, right, we don't have full visibility into what will happen for the full year 2026, especially in the back half of the year. You know, and we'll continue to monitor new activity as it shows up and the conversion of those permits and those wells that have been spud.
I would say generally, we're extremely pleased with the third-party exposure and especially the complement that provides to the concentrated exposure through the Diamondback drill bit.
Betty Jiang
Senior Equity Research Analyst of US Integrated Oil and E&Ps, Barclays
Yeah. Those are really encouraging signs to see. My second question is on AI. It strikes me that the royalty model is ideally positioned to benefit from AI integration, and thinking about the impact on predictive nature of future activity, maybe deal valuation. Can you just speak to how you see the tools that are available today could potentially impact your operations and M&A?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, Betty. I mean, I would say generally, you're correct, right? There's a lot of data flowing through the mineral business. There's a lot of data on 35,000 wells throughout the Permian that can be utilized for a lot of things, right? We can use that data to make operational changes to, you know, to buy more minerals in areas where something is emerging.
You know, I think in the near term, some of the benefits of AI and automation and machine learning is really to make our business more efficient on the back end, right? Tracking 35,000 wells every month is not, should not be a manual process. We're working to, you know, move everything from, you know, manual to automated.
You know, and then beyond that, it's about, you know, finding a way to utilize all this data effectively and efficiently. You know, even potentially monetize it should we not see that it provides us a differential advantage. I think it can provide a lot of data to the market. For now, we're gonna keep it all internal and I think focus on some of the automation, and that's actually one of the synergies that the Sitio team brought to the table that we hadn't developed ourselves at Viper.
With all these deals, we end up learning something. I'd say the biggest thing from the Sitio team has been, you know, big data and automation.
Betty Jiang
Senior Equity Research Analyst of US Integrated Oil and E&Ps, Barclays
Very interesting. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Neil Mehta of Goldman Sachs & Company. Your line is open.
Neil Mehta
Head of Americas Natural Resources Equity Research, Goldman Sachs & Co
Yeah. Thanks so much. You just congrats on some of these non-Permian divestitures. It's good to see the business kind of core up around the Permian again. You know, as we think about the cash that's coming in, Kaes, are there any considerations we should be mindful of in terms of the number that's coming in? Are there any offsets, whether it's taxes or anything else around these inflows?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, we kind of highlighted that there would be a little bit of a tax hit. I think our net proceeds would be about $610 million. There'll be some reduction, between, you know, effective date and close date. All in all, you know, I think it generally, the proceeds are gonna pay down essentially the revolver to zero as well as, almost pay our term loan down to, essentially zero.
That would put, essentially a balance sheet, I define as almost perfect position with, you know, one five-year note, one 10-year note, that we executed over the summer, you know, leaving us a lot of optionality and flexibility to, you know, buy little deals, but also, you know, return a lot of cash to shareholders.
Neil Mehta
Head of Americas Natural Resources Equity Research, Goldman Sachs & Co
Yeah. Kaes, can you talk about the A&D market? You know, that's been a kind of a hallmark of the broader Diamondback complex is finding those bolt-on opportunities. Do you think, especially given the softer commodity price environment, does that make it easier or harder to get deals done here over the next six to 12 months?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, traditionally it makes mineral deals harder to get done. It's, you see a lot more upstream deals lower in the cycle than minerals just because of the zero CapEx nature of minerals. I think we're probably on a bit of a pause at Viper for now and waiting for, you know, what we see as a still a significant opportunity set to come our way in the coming years. Austen, anything else you want to add?
Austen Gilfillan
President, Viper Energy
Yeah, I think that's certainly the case on the larger, more strategic acquisitions. You know, we've tried to position ourselves to be the consolidator of choice on the, you know, the billion-dollar-plus type opportunities. It's, it's tough to see those transacting with where commodity prices are today. I would say it's a little bit different on kind of the smaller ground game type acquisitions.
We've had some success and some of those owners, you know, might see their royalty checks go down and see that as an opportunity to liquidate it. You know, that's tougher to scale today relative to the size of the enterprise value, at least. Part of our thinking additionally is with the buyback, that's an effective way to buy really high quality assets that we know and that are growthy assets today.
It's kind of a combined, you know, strategy of how to deploy capital for us today.
Neil Mehta
Head of Americas Natural Resources Equity Research, Goldman Sachs & Co
Yep. Thanks, Austen. Thanks, Kaes.
Austen Gilfillan
President, Viper Energy
Thank you.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Thanks, Neil.
Operator
Our next question comes from Kalei Akamine of Bank of America. Your line is now open.
Kalei Akamine
Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, good morning, guys. Kaes, in your opening remarks, you called out that Viper has been exposed to about half of all third-party activity in the Permian Basin over the last three years. In the basin this year, there's been a reduction in activity because of oil price uncertainty. The market expects maybe zero oil growth from the Permian Basin next year, yet your Permian volumes continue to grow. That's a favorable dynamic. How long do you expect that it can continue?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
I mean, I think the immediate nature of the Diamondback Viper relationship probably drives that growth for, you know, at least the next couple of years, if not, if not longer. I think we have somewhere between a 5% and 7% interest expected in all of Diamondback's wells on average for the next, you know, five years. That's a pretty unique position to be in. I think, you know, that combined with the, in our, in our remarks, we kind of highlighted that that combined with the broad exposure, otherwise, you know, puts us in a pretty good spot here for the next few years.
Kalei Akamine
Analyst, Bank of America
I appreciate that. For my next question, one question that we get from investors concerns the valuation of Viper. It's the best risk-adjusted return in the Permian in our view. Another way to look at it is that VNOM shares are trading with great value today. My question is, would you ever consider using free cash at bank to purchase more interest in VNOM shares?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, it's certainly on the table. I think Diamondback has some strategic priorities that they need to continue to execute on, you know, mainly reducing its share count as well. You know, we certainly are kind of trying to pound the table on VNOM's valuation. Also I think, you know, as part of the rationale for the non-Permian asset sale getting executed so quickly is that we can lean in at the Viper level and reduce that Viper share count.
You know, I think until the market wakes up to the free cash flow yield plus growth story, you know, we're gonna try to take advantage of it as a complex.
Kalei Akamine
Analyst, Bank of America
I appreciate the comments. Thanks, Kaes.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Derrick Whitfield of Texas Capital. Your line is now open.
Derrick Whitfield
Head of Energy Equity Research, Texas Capital
Thanks. Good morning, all, and thanks for taking my question. For my first question, I wanted to start with your guidance regarding the soft guide for 2026. How are you thinking about the price sensitivity associated with that guidance from a Diamondback operating perspective?
Austen Gilfillan
President, Viper Energy
Yeah. That really contemplates the base case of Diamondback's, you know, current activity levels, right? Really maintaining that more maintenance level through 2026. To draw on their analogy, you know, being in the yellow light scenario, that's kind of what's underwritten here, being it could flex up or down.
I think the beauty of the relationship, and Kaes was hitting on it earlier, to the extent that it flexes down, you know, Diamondback will really be prioritizing the highest returning projects in the lower commodity price environment. Viper tends to be insulated, at least in gross, reductions in Diamondback activity level and, you know, just kind of gets a higher percent exposure and a higher average NRI.
Derrick Whitfield
Head of Energy Equity Research, Texas Capital
Got it. Makes sense. Maybe just to build on an earlier question. With the benefit of more time with the Sitio team and their approach, could you guys elaborate on the synergy opportunity you see from a cash savings perspective on just implementing some of the AI processes, and then the opportunity it could generate from a ground game perspective?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah. I would say, you know, obviously, you know, the employee aspect of the deal and those synergies have been realized, and we brought over some select high performers from Sitio that are helping us out today. You know, second to that, one of the big synergies was cost capital savings on the debt, on both their debt and ours. You know, it was clear that Viper got upgraded to investment grade and was able to execute its first investment grade deal in the quarter in July.
That sets us up from a balance sheet perspective. You know, I think on the automation side, there's certainly benefits to automating the processes at Viper.
I think over time, those same people that are working on automating those processes at Viper will then move to automate more at Diamondback. It's kind of a synergy to the, to the parent co as well. I can't tell you exactly what that number's gonna be today, but I think a lot of our business is gonna be moving towards, you know, less manual entry and more, you know, observing by, you know, exception versus doing things by hand. I think a lot to come there. I think the whole industry is working to continue to automate, but you can expect us to be on our front foot.
On, you know, on the deal side, I think, I think we, you know, being in Midland, we have pretty good access to all the deals. There's a saying out here that if a deal leaves Midland, that means it might not be a good deal. You know, we're on the front foot here in the mix and, you know, we have really good deal flow.
Derrick Whitfield
Head of Energy Equity Research, Texas Capital
Great color. I'll turn it back to the operator.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Leo Mariani of ROTH. Your line is now open.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH
Hi, guys. I just wanted to clarify on the guidance here. I know it's soft guide for 2026. When you guys talk about mid-single digit, you know, growth, you know, next year versus Q4, I assume that's, you know, kind of unadjusted, you know, for the pending asset sale. Clearly as we strip those volumes out, then, you know, you kind of wouldn't quite hit that mid-single digit growth. It'd be a little bit lower. That's kind of a pre-asset sale guide here.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah. I mean, if you look at Q4 being pro forma, right? Really the way to look at it is you're gonna have a couple thousand barrels a day of growth on an absolute basis on the assets that we'll retain. The Q4 guidance of 66,000 a day of oil at the midpoint that includes about 5,000 a day of contribution to the non-Permian assets. If you strip that out, that'll be your go forward starting point for 2026, and then you'll grow a couple thousand barrels from there, which kind of gets you to that mid-single digit level.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH
Okay. Appreciate that clarification. Obviously, you've got the asset sale done, and you sprintly spoke to returning a greater percentage of capital, you know, to shareholders. You clearly leaned into the buyback, you know, pretty heavily, but just trying to get a sense, you know, as that debt is paid off, as you kind of spoke to, sounds like in the next handful of months, are your eyes also looking to maybe kind of, you know, accelerate the growth, you know, in the variable dividend, you know, component as well over the next few quarters? Is that something that investors should also be looking forward to?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah. I mean, I think it's all price related, right? The key point here on the buyback, which is, you know, in our mind, our third priority return of capital behind the base dividend and the variable dividend, you know, leaning into that buyback, you know, sends a pretty strong message that we think the stock's cheap. You know, we do agree with a lot of our large shareholders, Diamondback being the largest, that we want a majority of the return of capital in the form of cash. I think what's interesting about Viper with the debt position it's in, the balance sheet position it's in, is that it can do both.
you know, I think we would at some point tap the brakes on the buyback if the market wakes up to this story. Until then, we're gonna keep reducing the share count.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH
All right. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Tim Rezvan from KeyBanc Capital Markets. Your line is now open.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Thanks for taking my questions, folks. I don't mean to beat the dead horse here, you know, the repurchase news was really notable. You know, it was equal to your prior two biggest quarters combined. Is it safe to say this was more of kind of an extreme quarter, given, you know, shares at the 37, 38 level? Would you potentially look to go, you know, even bigger at the expense of the variable dividend if you thought the dislocation warranted that?
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah, I mean, Tim, I think it depends, right? I think what's interesting about, again, about Viper, here we are at, you know, $60 oil generating 92%, 93% margins. There's a lot of flexibility to do a lot of things with cash, right? I think if you put your E&P hat on, you're restricted by how much capital you need to spend to maintain your production base. In here, other people are spending capital for you to maintain your production base. That frees up a lot of free cash to do different things with.
You know, I think, if the market dislocates further, we can lean in further without compromising, you know, free cash flow generation or the balance sheet.
It's truly, you know, in my mind, it should theoretically be a lower cost capital business than where it's trading today.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay. Okay. I appreciate that response. Then on the topic of repurchases, you know, there's been some market consternation, you know, perhaps overdue about these new holders that you have following the Sitio closing, and I believe there's four, you know, what people would call unnatural holders at about 13% of shares. Can you talk, Kaes, about any dialogue you've had with any of them and how high that is on your sort of, you know, kind of maybe removing that overhang or sort of addressing that as they look to sell? Thank you.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Yeah. We'll be prepared to address it should they make the decision to sell. You know, in talking to a lot of them, you know, particularly with respect to the Sitio merger, you know, they merged their stock into ours knowing that there's a lot of long-term upside to the combined business. I can't comment on if they want to or don't want to sell because that's their decision. I will say, you know, we have the firepower to aid that if that ever happened.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Just like any other shareholder, right? If there are any other large shareholders looking to sell here, we've got the firepower to buy those shares back.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay. That's all I had. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. I am showing no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn it back to the CEO, Kaes Van't Hof, for closing remarks.
Kaes Van't Hof
CEO, Viper Energy
Thanks, everybody, for participating today. Please reach out if you have any questions, and we'll talk to you in one quarter.
Operator
Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program, and you may now disconnect.
